sections.h2: Selling a house in Mount Vernon
sections.html:
Skagit County's seat sits in the river valley about 60 miles north of Seattle and 51 miles south of the Canadian border. The July 1, 2025 estimate is 35,193 residents. An agent, a sale on your own and an as-is cash bid all lead to the same finish: a deed, an excise tax affidavit and a recording with Skagit County.

About 60.3 percent of homes are owner-occupied, with a median value of $472,300. Median gross rent is $1,405 and median household income is $75,777. Medians cover the whole city, so price from recent sales close to your address. Because the Skagit River runs beside downtown, flood zones come up early in most sales, and the next section covers that.

sections.h2: Flood zones and the Skagit River
sections.html:
Many Mount Vernon properties sit in the 100-year floodplain. The city tells owners to check FEMA's Map Service Center or ask Development Services for the zone and what it means for a parcel. Learn your zone before listing day, since buyers and lenders ask early.

Do these three things early:

  • Find the parcel on FEMA's Map Service Center, or have the city name the flood zone.
  • Gather any elevation certificate, flood insurance policy or past claim records.
  • Answer the seller disclosure questions on flooding, standing water and floodplains from what you know.

The city finished a permanent flood wall in 2019, but a buyer will still want your records, not a story. Rain falls mostly from October through March, so show that gutters, drainage and crawl space are in good order.

sections.h2: Permits to check before you list
sections.html:
Development Services is at 910 Cleveland Avenue, phone 360-336-6214, email permittech@mountvernonwa.gov. The Building Division reviews permits, interprets codes, inspects work and enforces the code. The city uses the 2021 International Codes with Washington amendments. This is how common projects are treated:

ProjectPermit rule
Detached one-story shed or playhouse, 200 square feet or lessNo building permit, but a planning permit is still required
Retaining wall up to 4 feet from the bottom of the footingNo building permit unless it holds a surcharge
Deck 30 inches or less above grade and not over a basementNo building permit when a location permit is obtained
Fence under 7 feetPlanning permit from Development Services
Fence 7 feet or tallerBuilding permit
Re-roof with a single existing layer and no deck repairNo building permit

New fences and replacements always need one or the other. If a past remodel never had a permit, ask the permit technicians how to fix that before a buyer's inspector brings it up. Bring the address and a short description of the work, plus any photos or receipts you kept, so staff can tell you what is on file and what a resolution would involve. Doing this before you list keeps the surprise out of the inspection period.

Two county offices handle your closing. The seller signs a Real Estate Excise Tax Affidavit with the deed, the treasurer receives the tax, and state law sends the deed to the county auditor for recording.

The state portion has four bands. Closings through December 31, 2026 pay 1.1 percent on the first $525,000, then 1.28 percent to $1,525,000, 2.75 percent to $3,025,000 and 3 percent beyond. From January 1, 2027 the bands start higher, at $551,000, $1,551,000 and $3,051,000. The local portion is extra. Notarizing the deed fixes the sale date for the Department of Revenue, and payment is owed that day.

Skagit County's Treasurer can confirm the local rate and tell you what to bring. Raise the current half of the property tax with that office too.

The form under RCW 64.06.020 reaches the buyer five business days after the contract is accepted, unless the buyer waives it or the sale is exempt. Flooding, standing water, drainage and floodplain are all asked about. Answer from what you know, and where something happened, say when. A vague answer invites follow-up questions.

sections.h2: Selling an older Mount Vernon house
sections.html: Interstate 5 was built through downtown in 1969 and separated downtown from most of the residential district, so location within town shapes how buyers see a street. The city runs on a mayor-council form, with a seven-member council, so code changes pass through meetings you can attend. If your house is older, expect its age, any past flood history and its permit file to be the topics a buyer raises first. Pull the paperwork together before the first showing.

Interstate 5 cuts through downtown, and State Route 9 runs parallel to it, with State Routes 536 and 538 linking downtown and the Baker Heights area. Skagit Station connects Amtrak Cascades, Skagit Transit, Greyhound and local taxis, and a commuter bus runs to Everett Station for the Sounder train. Workers average 22.9 minutes getting to work. Mention whichever of these is closest to your house, and give the walking or driving distance if it is short. Bellingham International Airport is 25 miles north, which some buyers care about.

sections.h2: What happens after an accepted offer
sections.html:
After an offer is accepted, the sequence is predictable. A contract is signed and the disclosure form goes out. A title company opens the file and orders a settlement statement. You sign the deed and the affidavit, and the tax gets paid. The county then records the deed and the funds are released.

A cash purchase leaves out the buyer's loan, which removes one common cause of delay. Gather your flood records now, as the sections above suggest, so nothing waits on you.

Three situations point toward it: the house is in a flood zone and you want no financing contingency, repairs are overdue, or you inherited a home and want to close on your own schedule.

Before agreeing, make the buyer verify funds, put the closing date on paper, and name who pays excise tax and title fees. Then run the comparison against a listing by taking off excise tax, agent fees and repair credits, and counting the weeks the house would sit on the market. A request for an offer on your address shows where it lands.

If you take a listing instead, the buyer's inspector will likely ask about floodplain status and any open permit, so the records you gathered earlier carry over.

faqs.q: Do I have to disclose flood risk when I sell a Mount Vernon house?
faqs.a: The statutory disclosure form asks about flooding, standing water, drainage problems and floodplain location, and you answer from your own knowledge. Many properties are in the 100-year floodplain, so check your zone with FEMA's Map Service Center or Development Services first.

faqs.q: Who handles permits for a Mount Vernon home?
faqs.a: Call the Development Services permit technicians at 360-336-6214 or email permittech@mountvernonwa.gov. The office is at 910 Cleveland Avenue and can also tell you your zoning district and flood zone.

faqs.q: Does a fence need a permit in Mount Vernon?
faqs.a: Yes. All new fences and replacements need one: a planning permit under 7 feet and a building permit at 7 feet or taller.

faqs.q: How is the excise tax on a Mount Vernon sale figured?
faqs.a: State tax opens at 1.1 percent on the bottom slice and rises in bands, with a local rate added. For a total at your price, ask the Skagit County Treasurer or your title officer.

faqs.q: Is the excise tax due when the deed is recorded or when the sale happens?
faqs.a: The sale date controls, and the Department of Revenue means the day the deed is notarized, even if recording follows later. Wait more than a month after it and interest and penalties begin.
